newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Envoy pours oil on fiery U.S. ties with Colombia.
newsitem.headline: Envoy pours oil on fiery U.S. ties with Colombia.

text.p: U.S. Ambassador Myles Frechette has stirred a new controversy in already stormy U.S.-Colombia ties by saying Colombian drug lords offered to provide him with hard evidence of President Ernesto Samper's alleged links to the drug trade.

The shocking revelation, in an interview on Wednesday, marked the first public comment by a U.S. official on alleged offers by brothers Gilberto and Miguel Rodriguez Orejuela -- the jailed leaders of the Cali cartel -- to turn evidence against Samper as part of deal with U.S. judicial officials.

It came on the same day that Colombia said it was temporarily suspending a joint U.S.-Colombian drug crop eradication programme pending the revision of all bilateral cooperation agreements because of last week's decision by Washington to "decertify" Colombia for the second year as an ally in the war on drugs.
The Cali cartel is alleged to have financed Samper's 1994 election campaign with millions of dollars in drug money.

The cartel once held up to 80 percent of the world's cocaine trade, according to U.S. officials. Frechette has said the Rodriguezes continue running their empire from behind the walls of Bogota's La Picota prison.

"Yes, they told it to me," Frechette told the QAP television programme when asked if the Rodriguez brothers had ever tried to cut a deal by serving as stoolpigeons in the drug corruption trial that nearly forced Samper to step down.
"I answered back, through the same channels, that we weren't interested in reaching any agreement with them," he added. "What we want is that they be tried and punished for their crimes."
Frechette did not specify when the offer was made by the billionaire drug lords, arrested in 1995 and the target of an unsuccessful U.S. extradition request in 1996.

But he said Tony Seneca, a former station chief of the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) in Colombia who left the country early last year, had been approached by a son of Miguel Rodriguez with proposals "similar" to those made by the capos themselves through other go-betweens.
The younger Rodriguez offered to reveal all of the cartel's drug smuggling routes in exchange for a U.S. commitment to "stop persecuting" the drug mob's leaders, Frechette said.
"My government's response was a flat no," he said.

Samper was cleared by Colombia's Congress in June 1996 of any wrongdoing in connection with his campaign. But Assistant U.S. Secretary of State Robert Gelbard recently called him a "truly corrupt president."
Frechette insisted, in a separate radio interview on Thursday morning, that U.S. policy in Colombia was not aimed at "toppling Samper."
But the president's lawyer, Luis Guillermo Nieto Roa, said the United States, led by Gelbard and Frechette, would do anything to have Samper's head on a silver platter.

"If the Rodriguez brothers offered proof, it's a lie to say the American government would have rejected them," he said. "I'm sure that U.S. officials, led by Mr. Gelbard and Mr. Frechette, would have done anything possible to receive that proof," he added.
